To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
interleukin (IL) 17–producing cells are enriched in joints of children with juvenile idiopathic (juvenile onset) arthritis and are more frequent in the more severe form of this disease.

we have shown that IL-17–secreting cells are present in the synovium of patients with juvenile idiopathtic arthritis and that these cells have the capacity to produce a range of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines.

we have identified IL-17–expressing T cells in the synovium and peripheral blood of patients with JIA, and demonstrated that these cells have a migratory capacity toward the CCR6 chemokine ligand CCL20, which is highly expressed in the synovial tissue, and that the numbers of IL-17 T cells correlate with the clinical phenotype of JIA, suggesting their role in disease pathogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat arthritis.
identifying the cellular basis of the immune response in the joints of patients with arthritis.
the role of IL-17 in the pathogenesis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL-17–positive T cells are present in the synovial tissue in JIA and are enriched in the joint compared with the blood.
IL-17 producing T cell frequencies correlate with disease severity, but that the relationship between IL-22+ and IL-17+ cells is more complex and requires further investigation.
IL-17–expressing T cells are enriched at the site of inflammation in JIA and may contribute to joint destruction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Th17 cells are a novel subset of CD4+ T cells that are highly enriched in the joints in JIA.
the IL-17+ Th cell population is a major component of the T cell infiltrate in the synovium of JIA and that this population is associated with a more severe form of arthritis.
the Th17/Treg balance is a critical determinant of disease outcome in JIA.
The main takeaway from our work is that

IL-17–positive T cells are enriched at sites of inflammation in children with JIA and that their numbers correlate with disease severity, suggesting that these cells contribute to joint damage and disease outcome.
Th17 cells are present in the joint and are a significant source of proinflammatory cytokines.

the Th17 subset of T cells, which are characterized by their production of the pro-inflammatory cytokines interleukin 17 (IL- 17) and IL-22, may be a critical player in the pathogenesis of arthritis in children, and that the ratio of Th17 cells to regulatory T cells may be an important determinant of clinical disease.
